script.base: Detroit is a 3.5-point favorite in a 46-point game, so the base script is a competitive Lions lead with Jahmyr Gibbs closing it, not a blowout and not a shootout. Gibbs just carried 69 times for 313 yards over weeks 4, 5 and 7 (about 23 carries and 104 rush yards a game) with Sione Vaki at 7 carries and Jared Goff at 2, so the run game is Gibbs. Goff still has to throw to get to a 24.8 implied total: Amon-Ra St. Brown drew 33 targets, Jameson Williams 21, Sam LaPorta 20 and Gibbs 19 in that same three-game window. Minnesota, priced at 21.2, stays in the game long enough that Kyler Murray does not have to abandon Aaron Jones (53 carries, 233 yards in that window) for the whole afternoon, but Minnesota's dropbacks rise if they trail by a score. Pace is normal.
script.flip1: Detroit is up by two scores at half. Gibbs' carry count goes even higher, Goff's dropbacks shrink, and St. Brown, Williams and LaPorta yardage stalls the way a favorite-runs-the-clock script stalls quarterback and receiver props. Minnesota then abandons the run, so whichever Viking back is actually featured (Jones 53 carries or Jordan Mason 15 in the logged window; the board disagrees) loses his rushing line, and T.J. Hockenson, Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison targets spike late.
script.flip2: Minnesota's 71 percent blitz creates early negative plays, the Vikings lead, and Gibbs' rushing line dies while his checkdowns (19 targets, only 3 air yards in three games) and LaPorta or St. Brown targets rise. Murray's designed runs (13 carries, 116 yards in that window) stay live or grow if Minnesota is protecting a lead. The low-event version of the same blitz is a punt fest that drags the 46 total under and misses both receiving overs.

matchup.shell: No middle-of-field-open versus closed charting and no man-versus-zone rate is in the pack. Location yards per attempt is the proxy. Detroit allows 10.26 per attempt in the middle on 57 throws, 5.96 on the left (83) and 6.91 on the right (116). Minnesota allows 8.71 in the middle on 41 throws, 6.0 on the left (63) and 4.79 on the right (73). Both defenses bleed the middle and are finer outside, especially Minnesota to the right.
matchup.pressure: Minnesota blitzes 71 percent. Detroit blitzes 27 percent. No pressure rate, sack total or time-to-throw is saved, so it is not established that either blitz gets home. Detroit's offense is better when blitzed (0.38 EPA per dropback) than when not blitzed (0.24), so Minnesota's blitz identity has been a plus for this Lions offense, not a kill shot. Minnesota's offense is worse when blitzed (minus 0.17 EPA per dropback versus plus 0.06 with no blitz), and Detroit rarely brings extra rushers, so that weakness is mostly unused in the base script.
matchup.bleeds: Detroit's pass defense bleeds the middle at 10.26 yards per attempt and shows 29 tagged 20-plus pass events for 277 yards over six games, versus Minnesota's 12 events for 198. Those yard totals do not average to 20, so only the event counts are used, and cautiously. Detroit also allows 4.30 yards per carry and 18 runs of 10-plus. Minnesota allows 4.16 yards per carry and only 14 runs of 10-plus in six games, so the Viking run front is not a bleed; the pass soft spot is the middle, not the boundary.
matchup.overlap: Minnesota's volume primary in the logged window is Hockenson (19 targets, 161 yards, 123 air yards) running into Detroit's 10.26 middle. That is the textbook overlap, but his last four are 11, 119, 7 and 35, and the three-game total of 161 leaves the in-window games as 119, 7 and 35, so the mean is a one-game spike. That over is a dropped lean, not a leg. The selected overlap is on the Detroit side. LaPorta (20 targets, 190 yards, 174 air yards, 8.7 air yards per target) works the intermediate area into Minnesota's 8.71 middle. Gibbs' 19 targets came with 3 air yards total, the checkdown answer if Minnesota's blitz actually arrives. Williams (343 air yards on 21 targets, 16.3 air yards per target) does not attack Minnesota's weak spot; the Viking right side is their best zone at 4.79, and they have only 12 explosive-pass events in six games.

pre_mortem: It is Monday and both lost because Minnesota's 4.16 yards-per-carry front and 14 runs of 10-plus in six games showed up as the 68-yard Gibbs game again, while Goff's answers to the 71 percent blitz went to St. Brown (33 targets, 329 air yards in three games) and Williams (343 air yards) instead of the middle, so LaPorta posted the 18. Detroit also could have led by two scores early, fed Gibbs a fine rush total, and still left 123.5 short if the checkdowns never came, because rush-plus-rec needs both pieces and minus 115 was just juice on a 50/50 fair. The same clock-kill kills LaPorta at minus 113 with no price edge to bail out a script miss. That counter is why LaPorta is a lean and why Gibbs is strong rather than a max bet. It is not stronger than 23 carries plus a 63-yard tight end mean into an 8.71 middle, so both legs stay.

Gibbs rush-plus-rec over 123.5 is the touch monster that survives a Detroit lead or a Minnesota lead. LaPorta receiving over 45.5 is the intermediate answer on those same dropbacks.
